briefs.headline: Industry seeks LTCG, STT cuts in Budget 2027; MSME relief also on wish list
briefs.deck: Several industry bodies have been meeting top officials of the Finance Ministry as part of the annual pre-Budget consultation process
briefs.bodyText:
Several industry bodies have recommended to the Ministry of Finance that the upcoming Budget 2027 should rationalise the Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax rate on equities and reduce the rate of the Securities Transaction Tax (STT).
Officials in the Finance Ministry, including Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Revenue Secretary Arvind Shrivastava, have been conducting their pre-Budget consultative meetings, during which they met the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI), and the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM), among others.
Need to remove double taxation
One of the most-cited requests from the industry was the rationalisation of LTCG on equities. In Budget 2026, the Centre removed the 12.5% LTCG tax in the government securities market for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) alongside other measures including reforms under the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).
Currently, foreign and domestic investors have to pay 12.5% tax on the sale of equities on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh per annum on listed shares. The Centre has held several meetings with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and other industry players.
“Removing the LTCG levy would raise post-tax returns and close a gap with Korea, Taiwan and Brazil,” Rakesh Nangia, chairman of task force on International Taxes at ASSOCHAM said. “The debt market is a useful precedent, which after the G-sec relief, saw FPI inflows rise to about $9 billion in June-July.”
The PHDCCI has requested that the government abolish LTCG tax on equity investments, reduce the short-term capital gains (STCG) tax rate from 20% to 10%, and lower STT rates “to encourage long-term investment and improve India’s capital market competitiveness”.
In its representation to Ms. Sitharaman, FICCI highlighted the fact that foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn about Rs 3.08 lakh crore during the year. It added that capital gains tax, which is charged over and above the STT, erodes returns from equities, and needs a review to make India a more attractive place to invest.
However, other market players highlight that the revenue loss incurred from the removal of LTCG could be negated through a hike in STT. According to estimates by SBI Research, the removal of LTCG would result in a revenue loss of Rs 40,000-50,000 crore for FY28.
Computation as a key challenge
One of the key frictions for FPIs underscored by industry bodies and equity analysts is the computation of the tax. Under Income-Tax Act, the calculation of the LTCG is in the Indian rupee. The challenge arises due to currency depreciation as against the investor’s base currency during the holding period, due to which investors are still liable to pay tax even when net returns in dollar terms are flat or even negative. This issue is currently under examination.
VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Financial Services also cautioned against selective relief, noting that abolishing LTCG solely for FPIs would be discriminatory against domestic retail and direct equity investors who remain subject to the 12.5% tax. He urged any tax relief must apply equally across the board to ensure a level playing field.
Profits and currency as anchors
Industry experts also suggest that while amendments in tax laws are just one part of attracting inflows, what remains important is continued momentum in corporate earnings growth, policy certainty and a stable rupee.
As such, simplifying onboarding and setting one predictable tax clearance process at exit coupled with making dispute resolution faster and binding is what would bring stable long-term investments, Nangia noted.
Help for MSMEs
Budget 2027 will be presented against the backdrop of the ongoing West Asia crisis, rising inflation, and fiscal pressure on the government. In this, India’s micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) need help, the industry bodies have argued.
Towards this, PHDCCI has requested the Finance Minister to extend the overdue period after which a loan is classified as a non-performing asset (NPA) from 90 to 180 days “to accommodate longer working capital cycles and delayed realisation of receivables”.
Further, the chamber has called for an enhancement of PM MUDRA loan limits and a Budget announcement of direct equity support to MSMEs through the Fund of Funds Scheme, “with dedicated allocations for start-up seed capital and SME IPO participation.

briefs.headline: How much Venezuela oil can India realistically buy as Russia remains biggest supplier?
briefs.deck: India’s attraction for the US lies in its sophisticated refining capacity. However, replacing Russian supplies on a significant scale is not straightforward: refinery compatibility, prices, shipping costs and commercial viability will influence whether Indian refiners buy more Venezuelan oil. How much Venezuelan crude can India realistically buy?
briefs.bodyText:
The Donald Trump administration wants India to buy more crude oil from Venezuela. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent visit to India to discuss the possibilities with Reliance clearly shows America’s push to increase the market for Venezuelan supplies while encouraging India to diversify away from Russian oil.
Russia, however, remains India’s biggest crude oil supplier, having gained a substantial share of the country’s imports after Indian refiners stepped up purchases of discounted Russian barrels. The US has repeatedly pressed New Delhi to reduce its reliance on Russian energy, making India’s oil sourcing an important issue in bilateral trade and diplomatic negotiations.
India’s attraction for the US lies in its sophisticated refining capacity. Reliance’s Jamnagar complex can process heavy Venezuelan grades that many refineries cannot easily handle.
Rubio has called India a refining superpower. Expanding purchases could give Venezuelan oil a larger market while offering India another source of crude.
However, replacing Russian supplies on a significant scale is not straightforward: refinery compatibility, prices, shipping costs and commercial viability will influence whether Indian refiners buy more Venezuelan oil. How much Venezuelan crude can India realistically buy?The difficulty with Venezuelan oil
The biggest problem is that Venezuelan crude oil is not easy to refine.
Analysts note that the first problem is its viscosity: Venezuela’s extra-heavy crude needs to be diluted with naphtha or condensate just to move it through pipelines and export it.
Then comes the high sulphur content and large residue yield, which require sophisticated refining equipment to turn the oil into valuable fuels.
“This is crude that suits complex refineries, but not every refinery can handle it economically,” Natalia Katona, Commodity analyst tells TOI.
Quality consistency is another concern, she notes.
Why is Venezuelan crude difficult to refine?
The crude is high in metals such as vanadium and nickel and in acidity, which poison catalysts and corrode equipment.
Naveen Das, Senior Crude Oil Analyst at Kpler says that more than half of each barrel is residue, the thick bottom fraction that must be cracked or coked to make diesel and gasoline.
“Only complex refineries with cokers, hydrocrackers and ample hydrogen can earn a margin on it,” he tells TOI.
Variations between cargoes, including water content, can make handling and processing more difficult. In some cargoes water content may reach 5%, which adds another operational challenge: buyers need both the equipment and the experience to manage those cargoes.
How much can India really buy?
According to Kpler data, India imported 4.71 million barrels per day of crude in August and 5.33 million barrels per day in September. Venezuela’s share was 7.4% at the August peak, 3.7% in September and 5.7% in October.
“At 450-500 thousand barrels per day on an import base of about 5.2-5.5 million barrels per day, a realistic share is 6-9%. That would match or modestly exceed the 6.7% share recorded in FY18. A share near 10% would need more than 500 thousand barrels per day, which Venezuela’s current export base cannot supply without displacing most non-Indian buyers,” Naveen Das tells TOI.
Praveen Rai, Director at Grant Thornton Bharat estimates that India can realistically absorb around 400,000–550,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude on a sustained basis, with short-term volumes potentially approaching 600,000 bpd under favourable conditions.
“Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar complex would remain the principal buyer given its ability to process heavy-sour crude at scale. India has already demonstrated significant absorption capacity, with Venezuelan imports reaching around 444,000 bpd in August 2026,” he tells TOI.
Natalia Katona points to another limitation: there will be competition from Gulf countries.
“Reliance would do most of the heavy lifting, with IOC another potential buyer, because processing large volumes requires the ability to manage both the residue yield and sulphur. Jamnagar could substitute some Basrah Heavy by Venezuelan crude, but Iraq is much closer. If Iraqi barrels are available at competitive delivered prices, Venezuela has a harder case to make for Indian refiners,” Katona tells TOI.
The biggest competitive obstacle is the US Gulf Coast. Its refineries are well suited to Venezuelan crude and much closer to the loading ports.
However, the constraint is not simply India’s refining capacity.
Venezuela’s production and export availability, shipping economics, sanctions, and the discount of Venezuelan Merey relative to Russian Urals and competing Middle Eastern grades will ultimately determine flows.
“Around 500,000 bpd represents a reasonable sustainable level for India, while 550,000–600,000 bpd is achievable during favourable market conditions. Sustaining volumes materially above that level would require higher Venezuelan production and broader participation from Indian refiners beyond Reliance,” Rai says.
In this case a natural question would be “can Venezuela simply produce more crude to satisfy both the US and Asian demand”?
“I would be cautious about assuming production can quickly reach 2 million b/d (as some market analytics assume). In my view, reaching 1.5 million b/d by 2030 would already be good news,” Katona says.
Does it make economic sense?
According to experts, the major question is how much discount as compared to Urals will be available to Indian refineries for processing this crude economically.
As Pankaj Srivastava, Senior Vice President, Commodity Market - Oil at Rystad Energy points out: Economics is based upon the configuration and complexity of the refineries and how refineries blend this crude and utilize higher production of coke.
In addition to that, how much comparable crude is with Russian Urals as freight, insurance and other changes would play a role in the landed cost of the crude.
Also, Indian Refineries are operating at 105-110% utilization rate. Hence, higher portions of Venezuelan crude can hamper the refinery runs.
Let’s break this down further:
Naveen Das of Kpler is of the view that the oil makes sense for complex refiners, but the margin is narrower than it was.
It takes about 40 days via the Cape, and higher tanker rates remain a major risk to long-distance Venezuelan shipments.
“The September dip is consistent with that sensitivity. Where the coker margin on the residue plus the discount exceeds freight and the distillate yield penalty, as at Jamnagar, the barrel clears; for simple refiners it does not,” he tells TOI.
On the other hand, risks of Russian crude becoming costlier and carrying sanctions risk do improve Venezuela’s relative case.
Praveen Rai shares some important insights:
Indian customs data for August 2026 show Venezuelan crude, mainly imported by 
Reliance Industries
, landed at 66 dollars per barrel, a 24 dollar per barrel discount to the Indian Crude Basket (ICB) on a delivered basis, compared with 88 dollars for Russian and 93 dollars for Iraqi and Arab Light grades.
The headline discount can be eroded by freight since Venezuela is roughly twice as far as Russia and about five times as far as the Middle East!
“Industry estimates suggest a discount of about $10-14 per barrel to Brent is needed to offset freight, insurance, and higher processing costs,” he tells TOI.
“For complex private refiners, value comes from deep conversion as much as from cheaper feedstock. With most barrels allocated to US refiners and Reliance, and sales governed by US licences and Treasury-controlled accounts, refiners should treat Venezuelan crude as an opportunistic margin boost rather than guaranteed supply,” he cautions.
Natalia Katona believes that while it may make some economic sense to buy crude from Venezuela, the freight bill consumes most of the headline discount!
Current assessments put Merey at around $36/bbl below ICE Brent on an FOB basis, with $32–34/bbl for VLCC freight to India. That leaves only $2-4/bbl of the discount before insurance, handling and the additional processing costs, she tells TOI.
“For such a long voyage, VLCCs provide the necessary scale, as smaller tankers generally make the economics harder. By contrast, Aframax freight from Venezuela to the US Gulf Coast is assessed at around $9-10/bbl. Those shorter voyages can also allow direct delivery and avoid some of the ship-to-ship transfers that larger vessels destined to far away freight require,” she adds.
The bottom line
The clearest case for significantly more Indian buying would be another deterioration in Middle Eastern supply, leaving fewer alternative heavy grades available. Even then, Indian refiners would have to bid competitively against US buyers.
Natalia Katona’s view is that this diplomatic significance is larger than the likely increase in physical volumes. This way, Venezuelan oil will remain a relatively small part of India’s diversification strategy.
“In my view, neither India nor the US has much appetite for a substantial increase in actual shipments to Indian refiners,” she concludes.
India may have stepped up crude oil purchases from Venezuela as part of its diversification strategy and the US may be actively pushing for India to buy it, but ultimately refining constraints, competition from America for the same barrels, Venezuela production constraints will be big factors that will weigh.
For now, Russia is likely to continue being the single largest supplier and as supplies from the Middle East normalise, Venezuelan crude may find its place among the top suppliers, but it is unlikely to go beyond single to early double digits in terms of share. Russia by contrast makes up over 35% of India’s crude oil imports: the difference is too stark to miss!

briefs.headline: Google launches two AI chips as it seeks to challenge NVIDIA’s dominance
briefs.deck: New systems target secure AI inference and memory-intensive workloads as Google seeks to expand enterprise adoption of its in-house AI processors
briefs.bodyText:
Google has expanded its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) portfolio with two new AI chip systems, stepping up its challenge to NVIDIA’s dominance in AI computing infrastructure.
The company unveiled TPU 8tx, designed for secure and confidential AI inference, and TPU 8i Max, built for memory-intensive workloads involving large context windows and increasingly sophisticated AI agents.
A TPU is Google’s custom-designed processor that accelerates AI workloads, including training and running large language models, more efficiently than general-purpose chips.
The launch is part of Google’s strategy to expand its custom accelerators beyond its own data centres and attract external customers. Its TPU business now has nearly 100 customers, including frontier AI laboratories, trading firms, retailers and universities.
A major challenge in competing with NVIDIA is overcoming dependence on its CUDA software ecosystem, which has long given its GPUs a competitive advantage. Google is addressing this through broader software compatibility. Last month, it open-sourced TorchTPU, enabling PyTorch code and Hugging Face models to run natively on its chips. It has also introduced an open-source TPU agent suite, currently in preview, supporting coding tools such as Claude Code, Cursor and Google Antigravity.
The TPU 8tx incorporates hardware-level security to protect data and AI models even during processing. This is aimed at enterprises and government agencies seeking to train or fine-tune models using sensitive proprietary information without exposing it.
The TPU 8i Max targets applications requiring extensive memory and processing capacity, including AI agents analysing large software codebases and lengthy videos. Google said it offers twice the computing capacity and memory bandwidth of its predecessor, TPU 8i.
The new systems complement TPU 8t, designed for AI model training, and TPU 8i, optimised for inference and real-time reasoning.
Google is also allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly in their own data centres, besides accessing them through Google Cloud.
The move reflects a broader industry shift towards custom AI chips to reduce dependence on external suppliers. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy with its Trainium processors through TorchNeuron, which enables PyTorch workloads to run with minimal code changes.

briefs.headline: Indian Railways rolls out Vande Bharat sleeper trains in 2026, plans some more soon
briefs.deck: Vande Bharat sleeper trains are fully air-conditioned overnight train services that have been designed to offer superior comforts to Rajdhani Express trains, while also reducing travel time with higher average speeds. A few days ago, the Vande Bharat sleeper trains were launched on the Delhi-Varanasi and Mumbai-Bengaluru routes.
briefs.bodyText:
2026 has been a milestone year for 
Indian Railways
 with the introduction of the Vande Bharat sleeper train services. Vande Bharat sleeper trains have been put into service so far on three routes.
A few days ago, the Vande Bharat sleeper trains were launched on the Delhi-Varanasi and Mumbai-Bengaluru routes. Earlier this year, the first Vande Bharat sleeper train was introduced between Howrah and Guwahati.
Vande Bharat sleeper trains are fully air-conditioned overnight train services that have been designed to offer superior comforts to Rajdhani Express trains, while also reducing travel time with higher average speeds.
More Vande Bharat sleeper trains soon
Indian Railways has given BEML the contract to manufacture 10 Vande Bharat sleeper trains to begin with. Six out of these have been manufactured and the remaining four are being made.
Sources told TOI that two more rakes are expected to be rolled out this month and the other two will be ready in the coming two months.
BEML has also been tasked with manufacturing an additional three rakes of Vande Bharat sleeper trains for which the process of procuring the necessary supplies and raw materials has started.
Meanwhile, BEML is also manufacturing India’s first high-speed bullet train for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train corridor. 
A section of this stretch is expected to become operational in the second half of 2027.
Vande Bharat Sleeper Trains
Developed for long-distance journeys, the Vande Bharat Sleeper aims to bring together modern technology, enhanced safety features and passenger-oriented facilities to improve the experience of travelling overnight. Its design aims to make extended journeys more comfortable, with a focus on sleeping arrangements, hygiene, security, accessibility and convenience.
The train can run at speeds of 180 kmph and has been cleared for 160 kmph speeds, though the maximum speed on each route depends on the sectional clearance.
Passenger comfort and convenience have also been considered in the design. The train features ergonomically designed, odour-free toilets with vacuum evacuation, along with dedicated berths and toilets for differently-abled passengers.
Modern passenger amenities and spacious luggage storage areas are provided to make long journeys more convenient. Integrated BRL units come with a three-pin charging socket and switch, while Type A and Type C USB ports offer additional charging options.
In terms of power and performance, the train incorporates regenerative braking to improve energy efficiency, along with an under-slung propulsion system. Its advanced aerodynamic design is intended to support smoother acceleration and deliver a ride with minimal jerks.
The train's design features include an austenitic stainless steel car body that meets EN15227 crash standards. It has a fully sealed flexible gangway fitted with a quick-release mechanism, while centrally controlled single-leaf automatic sliding plug doors provide access between the train and its surroundings.
Noise insulation and mitigation measures are intended to create quieter passenger saloons. The interiors also feature direct and indirect LED lighting, as well as sensor-based intercommunication doors.
Safety and security provisions include compliance with EN45545 HL3-grade fire safety standards and fire barrier doors at the end walls. The train is equipped with a Train Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), disaster management lighting and a smoke and fire detection system (FDS). CCTV cameras support safety and passenger surveillance, while emergency push buttons allow passengers to raise an alarm when required.
A PAPIS-based communication system enables interaction among the driver, guard and passengers. First AC passengers have access to showers with hot water. The train also includes a Wi-Fi router with an access point network, while the driver's cab is air-conditioned and crew members have access to a dedicated toilet.
Indian Railways has also awarded the contract for manufacturing 50 Vande Bharat sleeper trains with more coaches to ICF. Additionally around 200 Vande Bharat sleeper trains with 16 coaches are being made by Kinet and Titagarh Wagons.

briefs.headline: MRF’s Q2 profit skids 27% as raw material costs squeeze margins
briefs.deck: Tyre maker anticipates continued disruptions and volatility in commodity markets. Raw material and logistics costs are expected to remain elevated.
briefs.bodyText:
MRF Ltd reported a 26.6% year-on-year (YoY) decline in consolidated net profit to ₹386.99 crore for the second quarter ended September 30, 2026, as a sharp rise in raw material costs eroded margins despite robust revenue growth.
Consolidated total income rose 17.4% to ₹8,791.58 crore during the quarter. However, profit before tax (PBT) fell 25.5% YoY to ₹521.81 crore. Earnings per share declined to ₹912.46 from ₹1,243.60.
The cost of materials consumed surged 43.1% YoY to ₹6,552.57 crore. Total expenses increased 21.8% YoY to ₹8,269.77 crore.
In its earnings statement, MRF said it had registered strong double-digit sales growth, supported by sustained demand from both original equipment (OE) and replacement segments.
However, “The steep increase in prices of raw materials due to global uncertainties adversely affected profitability during the quarter. Price increase and cost saving measures by the Company helped to mitigate cost pressures.”
Flagging continued uncertainty, the company said, “The company anticipates continued disruptions and volatility in commodity markets. Raw material and logistics costs are expected to remain elevated. We will continue to take measured steps to address these challenges.”

briefs.headline: Australia's Qantas to axe 850 jobs in offshoring deal with Accenture
briefs.deck: First round of cuts due by mid-2027; some corporate functions to be outsourced to Accenture ​in India and Australia; union accuses Qantas of going back on word against offshoring jobs
briefs.bodyText:
Qantas said on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) it would cut 850 jobs in Australia and outsource some corporate functions to consulting firm Accenture as it adapts to the increased use of artificial intelligence in the airline industry.
In an email to staff, Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson said the jobs would be cut “over the coming years”, with the first round to happen by mid-2027.
“I know this is hard news for some, and I’m sorry for the uncertainty it brings,” Ms. Hudson said. The job cuts affect around 3% of Qantas’ Australian workforce of 28,000.
The first phase of the cuts would affect finance, procurement, human resources and marketing staff. Some roles would be shifted to Accenture and performed by teams that would be “mostly” based in India.
The airline, Australia’s flag carrier, said the move was in response to rapid changes in the industry due to AI, and the Accenture partnership would help it overhaul its legacy systems and simplify some corporate functions.
“Through a partner we can access the data and AI skills that every industry in the world is competing for, because we cannot hire at the pace this work needs,” Ms. Hudson said.
Qantas is the latest in a growing number of big Australian companies to offshore workers in a bid to cut costs and improve efficiency. Woolworths, Officeworks, Telstra and National Australia Bank have announced similar moves this year.
The Australian Services Union said in a statement that Qantas had previously assured staff there was no plan to offshore jobs under the Accenture deal.
“Earlier this year, Qantas told us directly there was no plan to offshore any jobs. Today, they’ve come out and told hundreds of staff members that their work will now be delivered mostly from people overseas,” ASU Assistant National Secretary Scott Cowen said.
“Qantas staff have the right to an explanation.”
“AI is having a huge impact on workers across the country, but the cost of technology change should not be borne by the workers who have kept the airline running for years.”
A Qantas spokesperson denied giving such assurances to the ASU.
“We have never given assurances to the union that some jobs wouldn’t move offshore,” they said. “We have met with the union on a number of occasions over the last few months to discuss the potential for some roles to move to Accenture, with work to be delivered by their teams in India and in Australia.”

stories.headline: PT Usha takes IOA election battle to IOC, seeks probe into alleged violations
stories.deck: Usha, president of the Indian Olympic Association, has raised serious concerns over the SOM elections, demanding an independent inquiry from IOC president Kirsty Coventry due to alleged irregularities. In a confidential complaint, she detailed accusations of unethical campaigning and potential governmental interference.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president Usha has urged International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Kirsty Coventry for an independent examination of the IOA’s controversial Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elections.
In a confidential three-page complaint dated Nov 9, accessed exclusively by TOI, Usha raises serious concerns about the elections, including allegations of incumbent officials canvassing for candidates, messages seeking confirmation of voters’ participation and even references to the sports ministry in communications surrounding a secret ballot.
In the letter, Usha has also questioned the handling of her four representations by returning officer (RO) Sanjay K. Srivastava and asked the IOC to ascertain whether any govt or external influence was exerted during the electoral process.
The letter comes after Usha’s own electoral setback, with the IOA president finishing fifth with 40 votes in a six-way contest for four women’s SOM positions. Anju Bobby George topped the poll with 53 votes, followed by Rani Rampal (50), Dola Banerjee (45) and Saina Nehwal (43). Anitha Pauldurai secured six.
In her letter, Usha has clarified that her complaint is not intended to challenge the election result “merely because of its outcome”, nor is it directed against any individual on personal grounds. Instead, she has stated that it concerns “the conduct and oversight of the electoral process” and the need to uphold IOA autonomy.
Elaborating on her first allegation, Usha has written that WhatsApp communications circulated under the names of incumbent IOA executive committee members Dola Banerjee and 
Yogeshwar Dutt
 allegedly solicited votes for a particular panel, identifying four candidates by name and ballot details.
She stated that she brought these communications to Srivastava's attention, citing clauses 1.9 and 3.2 of the model code of conduct issued on Oct 30.
Quoting Clause 3.2, Usha pointed out that incumbent EC members “shall refrain from making public declarations” and “may in no way support a candidate”. She alleged that the communications raised concerns over compliance with the code and equal treatment of candidates.
Usha has also alleged that communications attributed to an incumbent IOA EC member raised concerns about voters being asked to confirm their voting activity. Separately, she referred to messages involving an individual identified to her as Sanjay Mishra, stated to be secretary of the badminton association, who allegedly asked athletes to confirm after voting and invoked the ministry through statements such as “from ministry” and “ministry is asking if we have confirmation msg.”
Questioning the reference to the ministry, Usha wrote: “I am not asserting that the ministry issued such an instruction.” However, she has asked the IOC to independently establish whether the ministry or any govt official sought information identifying voters or confirming their participation, and, if not, why its name was invoked. She stated that any such monitoring could undermine the independence and confidentiality expected in a secret-ballot election.
On the handling of her complaints, Usha has alleged that she submitted four separate representations to Srivastava during the election process but received “neither an acknowledgement nor a substantive response” to any of them. She has sought an examination of the RO’s handling of these representations and whether the mechanisms under the model code of conduct were effectively applied.
Invoking fundamental principle 5 and rules 27.6 and 2 of the Olympic Charter, Usha has argued that the concerns, if substantiated, go beyond an individual election dispute. She has also linked the issue to India’s ambition to host the 2036 Olympic Games, stating that the IOA must uphold the standards of “independence, transparency and good governance” expected within the Olympic movement.
Among her specific demands, Usha has asked the IOC to examine the alleged campaigning by incumbent EC members, investigate the reported requests for voting confirmations, ascertain whether any govt or external influence was exerted, and consider referring the matter to its relevant department, Ethics and Compliance Office or Ethics Commission. She has also sought corrective measures to safeguard future IOA elections.
Requesting confidentiality, Usha has stated that some information was shared by individuals who may be reluctant to come forward publicly. She said she had withheld private WhatsApp communications and identifying details of voters to protect them from possible repercussions, while offering to provide supporting material through an appropriate confidential channel. The letter was also copied to IOC officials James Macleod and Jérôme Poivey.
Usha had recently met Coventry on the sidelines of the Youth Olympic Games (YOG) in Dakar on Nov 2 and discussed India's Olympic and 2038 Asian Games bids.
Meanwhile, sources in Usha’s camp said she is neither contemplating approaching courts to challenge the SOM election outcome nor exploring the possibility of seeking nomination from an NSF to regain entry into the IOA general assembly as a voter. 
They said the camp’s hopes rest on IOC intervention following the complaint, alongside efforts to seek the PMO’s intervention into “alleged irregularities”.
Usha’s defeat followed an extraordinary withdrawal phase in which eight male candidates withdrew, leaving four elected unopposed, while five women withdrew, reducing the women's contest to six. All 80 voters eventually cast their ballots. Usha secured 40 votes, but her letter has now shifted the focus to the conduct and oversight of the election itself.

stories.headline: Sandpapergate row: Khawaja cancels media interviews after Cummins question
stories.deck: Usman Khawaja has canceled his remaining media interviews to promote his autobiography, Sabr. His decision follows a challenging interview with Sarah Ferguson where he faced questions about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Khawaja expressed concerns that future discussions would mainly revolve around this controversy rather than other aspects of his book. He emphasized the need for the entire…
stories.bodyText:
Former Australia opener 
Usman Khawaja
 has reportedly called off his remaining TV and radio interviews for the promotion of his autobiography, Sabr. The move follows a tough interview in which he was questioned about his claims surrounding the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, popularly known as Sandpapergate.
News Corp reported that publisher Penguin informed media outlets about the cancellations on Wednesday morning. This came after Khawaja faced questions from Sarah Ferguson on ABC's 7.30.
Khawaja is reportedly concerned that his future interviews will focus mainly on the ball-tampering controversy rather than the other subjects covered in his book.
During Tuesday's interview, he had already indicated that he did not want to discuss the allegations any further.
"I've talked on social media about this and I've written in my book, that's my statement, that's what it is, and I'm not going to really speak on any more of it at this moment in time," he said.
Khawaja refuses to answer question about Pat Cummins
During his conversation with Ferguson, Khawaja was asked about Warner backing his version of events and his statement that any "lies will eventually get out".
"What lies is he talking about?" she asked.
"I'm not going to speak on behalf of Davey," Khawaja replied.
"I've tried my best to tell my story in an open and safe environment."
Khawaja said he wanted the entire team to accept responsibility for the incident rather than leave three players to face the consequences.
"All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team, and I don't think that's a lot to say. I'm not asking a lot from people and I say, 'We were a part of it. That was us'. Let's just take accountability. I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt, and to stick with those three guys who were made out to be the only people who have taken it [accountability]," he said.
Ferguson also asked Khawaja whether Australia captain Pat Cummins knew about the use of sandpaper. However, the former opener did not answer the question.
"I'm not going to answer that."
He added: "I've written what I've written in my book. I've come out and stood by those three guys and told my account of what I saw."
Cummins, along with fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, had publicly denied knowing about the incident in 2021.
What did Khawaja claim about Sandpapergate?
Khawaja sparked a fresh debate on Saturday by claiming that the entire Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plan during the 2018 Test against South Africa in Cape Town. His statement is different from Cricket Australia's findings at the time, which held Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft responsible for knowing about the plan before it was carried out.
He also claimed that sandpaper had been used in the previous Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.
"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," he said ahead of the release of his book.
Khawaja, who retired this year after playing 88 Tests, has devoted an entire chapter of his autobiography to the scandal.
What punishments did Smith, Warner and Bancroft receive?
The Cape Town scandal had serious consequences for Smith, Warner and Bancroft. All three players were sent home following the incident. Smith received a 12-month ban and lost the Australia captaincy. Warner was also banned for 12 months and removed from leadership positions, while Bancroft received a nine-month suspension.
Khawaja believes the outcome might have been different if the entire team had accepted responsibility.
"I don't believe the whole team would have got a ban if we went in together," he said.
"I think it would have been shared. It's very hard to ban the whole team."
Khawaja denies making claims to boost book sales
Khawaja also rejected suggestions that he had made the revelations now to attract more buyers for his autobiography.
He told Ferguson that the ball-tampering issue was not part of the discussion when he signed his publishing deal in 2023. He also said his manager and publisher found out about the chapter only six months ago.
"Even when I gave it to them six months ago, they were shocked because I don't really talk about this to anyone," he said.
The former Australia opener also explained why he chose to share his account after retiring from international cricket.
"The reason I felt more comfortable saying it now is because I don't speak for the team anymore," he said.
"If I try to come out and do it while I'm still on the team, they have to look at me every day. We have to go operate as a team."
Cricket Australia responds to fresh allegations
Cricket Australia has responded to Khawaja's claims and defended the findings of its investigation. However, it also accepted that the inquiry was completed within a short period.
"The three players who received bans after the Cape Town Test acknowledged their breaches and accepted the penalties imposed," a spokesperson told Nine newspapers.
"We have acknowledged that the investigation was conducted in a short timeframe given the impending Test match and that there are varying opinions about some matters including the length of the sanctions imposed. We respect that players have different recollections of events from this time.
"But we remain comfortable the investigation's findings accurately reflect the statements and evidence provided at the time."
Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg has ruled out reopening the investigation.

stories.headline: Jannik Sinner plans late-December return at Saudi exhibition ahead of Australian Open
stories.deck: Sinner has not played since July when he beat Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final; he withdrew from the U.S. Open because of a right knee injury
stories.bodyText:
Jannik Sinner plans to return from injury at an exhibition event in December to prepare for the Australian Open and believes the enforced layoff has changed his attitude towards tennis.
Sinner has not played since July when he beat Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final. He withdrew from the U.S. Open because of a right knee injury.
Ongoing problems with the knee delayed the 25-year-old’s return and he announced last month his season was over.
Last week, Zverev took over the No. 1 ranking that Sinner held for 95 weeks.
“The aim is to go to Australia, the aim is also maybe to do a couple of tournaments first,” Sinner said at a sponsor event in Milan on Tuesday. “But I have to respect the protocols at the moment because if we rush things we could have more serious problems.
“I also only have that information, that I have to work hard every day for that objective and then we’ll see.”
One of those tournaments is the Six Kings Slam, an exhibition in Saudi Arabia that was postponed until late December because of the conflict in the Middle East.
“That (is the target) but we all know the situation what’s there at the moment, which is not the best, so this is not our decision as players, this is a more general decision,” Sinner told The Associated Press.
“But I think if we want to prepare for Australia (and) I’m not playing since Wimbledon, some matches before might be very helpful.”
The Six Kings Slam awards money but no ATP ranking points. Sinner won the second edition of the tournament last year.
The injury layoff has been the longest Sinner has been sidelined for and the five-time Grand Slam winner admits it has been such a difficult period for him that he hasn’t even been able to bring himself to watch much tennis.
“They haven’t been easy months, or rather they are not easy months, simply because I miss the competition, I miss going out onto the court, I really miss the thing I love doing: Playing tennis,” Sinner said.
“But in this very important moment taking care of my body is of the utmost importance, because I want to keep playing for another 10 or 15 years. So, if I end up returning to the court a month later, it doesn’t really change anything from that perspective.”
Sinner believes that when he is finally back on court he will see the sport in a different way.
“Before, it almost felt like the most normal thing in the world: You have a tournament, you win it, then you have another, you win it,” the Italian said. “Now, however, I’ve come to truly appreciate what I’ve managed to achieve.
“At the same time, my desire to win is even stronger, the urge to lift a major trophy — it’s the most wonderful feeling and the very thing we work so hard for. Previously, I took it all for granted, as if it were just the natural order of things; I hope to experience those emotions again .. and maybe I will enjoy everything even more.”
Sinner was asked if he had been using the enforced absence from tennis to broaden his horizons or learn a new skill.
“No unfortunately, this current period is really difficult because I’m at home, spending practically the entire day — every day — on a racing simulator,” said Sinner, who is a huge motorsport fan. “And then I head to the gym. When I get back, I jump straight back onto the simulator.
“I’ve always said that, in the future, you might see me behind the wheel of a race car. I want to get back on the court. It’s the first time I don’t have control, it’s strange and I don’t like it.”
One major thing Sinner has done during his absence from the court is make a coaching change.
Sinner announced last week that Darren Cahill will leave and Magnus Norman, former coach of Stan Wawrinka, has been hired to join his coaching team starting next month, working alongside Simone Vagnozzi.
“Magnus is someone very similar to Darren, though, of course, everyone is different,” Sinner said. “He’s the type of person who accepts the way we’re already working. That’s important because it’s crucial not to change everything all over again, but rather to focus on that 1% improvement each year to keep growing as a player.
“What I’ll miss most about Darren is definitely the personal part. We hit it off right from the start, and over time he became almost like a second father to me … whenever I faced difficult moments he was always one of the first people I would call.”
Cahill joined Sinner’s team in June 2022 and oversaw the Italian win five Grand Slam titles and achieve the No. 1 ranking.
He originally planned to step away after the 2025 season.
Cahill, who was also at the event with Sinner in Milan, highlighted the fact that he wrote on social media back in 2013 that Norman improves every single player he coaches.
“It’s really important that they have some clean air … So, no, I’m not going to be lurking next to Jannik over this coming period,” Cahill added. “It’s really important that I show the respect to Magnus as well, and that he can come in and form his relationship with this team and create his own memories.
“I wasn’t part of the due diligence that Jannik had in choosing the next coach. That was all him. He chose Magnus, but when he told me that was his choice I gave him a big thumbs up. I could not be more happy for him.”

stories.headline: Pant undergoing two-day simulation, likely to leave for New Zealand on November 12
stories.deck: Pant is one of the few cricketers in this current set-up, who has the experience of playing Test cricket in New Zealand when the national team toured that nation in 2020
stories.bodyText:
India's Test team is set to get a boost as star wicketkeeper batter Rishabh Pant in all likelihood will get fitness clearance from the BCCI Centre of Excellence and leave for New Zealand on Thursday.
Pant, who sustained a side strain while playing Irani Cup for Rest of India, was initially named in the India A squad for one unofficial Test subject to fitness. However, he didn't get the required 'RTP' (Return To Play) certificate from the CoE.
"Pant is completely fit. He is undergoing the match simulation drills at the CoE today and there is one round (of simulation) scheduled for tomorrow (Wednesday). Upon successful completion of both rounds, Pant will then leave for Wellington on November 12," a BCCI source privy to the development told PTI on conditions of anonymity.
Pant is one of the few cricketers in this current set-up, who has the experience of playing Test cricket in New Zealand when the national team toured that nation in 2020.
The 29-year-old Pant is one of the senior-most players in the set-up with 52 Tests under his belt. He has scored eight centuries and 21 fifties at an average of above 43. The left-hander has scored Test hundreds in Australia, England and South Africa among the SENA countries.

briefs.headline: New Zealand announce squad for India Tests: Who is in, who is out?
briefs.deck: The opening Test of the two-match series will be played at the Basin Reserve in Wellington from November 19. The second match will take place at Hagley Oval in Christchurch from November 27. Tom Latham will lead the New Zealand side.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: New Zealand have announced their squad for the two-Test series against India, with Devon Conway, Rachin Ravindra and Tom Blundell making the cut despite fitness concerns. All three players are hoping to be ready for the opening Test next week.
The opening Test will be played at the Basin Reserve in Wellington from November 19. The second match will take place at Hagley Oval in Christchurch from November 27.
Conway, Ravindra and Blundell race against time
Conway suffered a concussion following a collision with fast bowler Matt Henry during a training session before the ODI series against India. The opener is now trying to regain full fitness before the first Test.
Ravindra, meanwhile, has not played since dislocating his shoulder during a promotional shoot in September. The all-rounder suffered the injury while attempting a diving catch. As a result, he missed both the ODI and T20I series against India.
Blundell is also working his way back to fitness. The wicketkeeper-batter is recovering from a quadricep injury and has featured in just one domestic match since June.
Changes to the squad after England tour
New Zealand's last Test assignment was against England in June, where they won the series 2-1. 
Kane Williamson announced his retirement from international cricket after that series. Fast bowler Jacob Duffy has been added to the squad for the India Tests. Meanwhile, all-rounder Zak Foulkes and pacers Will O'Rourke and Ben Sears have missed out due to injuries.
Head coach Rob Walter said the team would aim to build on its success in England.
"The squad is largely consistent with the team that competed in England earlier this year, so it'll be great to be back together to try and recreate some of that success on home soil," Walter said.
"We've experienced great crowds so far during the white-ball series and we're really looking forward to having that support during the Tests."
New Zealand squad for India Tests
Tom Latham (captain), Tom Blundell, Devon Conway, Jacob Duffy, Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips, Rachin Ravindra, Mitchell Santner, Nathan Smith, Blair Tickner and Will Young.

briefs.headline: Ravi Shastri names this CSK pacer as Team India's workhorse for NZ Tests
briefs.deck: Anshul Kamboj has been highlighted by Ravi Shastri as a key player for India's upcoming Test series against New Zealand. Kamboj showed promise in ODIs despite a difficult Test debut, earning his place in the squad. Shastri emphasizes Kamboj's ability to bowl long spells and support teammates during challenging conditions. His capacity to move the ball and surprise batters strengthens India's fast…
briefs.bodyText:
Former India head coach 
Ravi Shastri
 believes young pacer Anshul Kamboj could play an important role in India's upcoming two-Test series against New Zealand. The first Test will begin in Wellington on November 19.
India have picked five fast bowlers in their 16-member squad for the series. They are Jasprit Bumrah, Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Kamboj.
Shastri feels the 25-year-old Kamboj has the qualities needed to succeed in New Zealand. He believes the Chennai Super Kings pacer can bowl long spells, keep things tight and support the other bowlers. Kamboj's batting ability is another advantage.
Shastri sees Kamboj as a workhorse
Shastri feels India will need a bowler who can bowl long spells and hold one end during difficult periods, especially in New Zealand's windy conditions.
"In a country like New Zealand, in Test match cricket, you will need a workhorse, and I think he is the man who could be your workhorse - someone like a Kamboj, who can come and bowl you those 15 overs and block one end up, especially when the going gets tough, when it's very windy and things of that sort," Shastri said on the Sony Sports Network.
"He can bat as well. So that comes in handy for Anshul. In the middle overs in a Test match or in an ODI game, you have got to have bowlers who have the ability to take wickets. 
Why India is 2-0 up is because of the performance of Anshul and Gurnoor Brar. In those middle overs where India normally go to spin to pick up wickets, it's the fast bowlers who have done the job," he added.
"He comes across as a bloke who has done a lot of bowling in domestic cricket for Haryana and across formats. I think he will be very useful in these conditions. Sometimes you have got to pick blokes as horses for courses. He is the kind of guy who hits the bat. He is accurate," Shastri said.
Kamboj impresses in ODIs after difficult Test debut
Kamboj's selection comes after a difficult start to his Test career. He made his debut against England but managed only one wicket while giving away 89 runs in 18 overs. He was dropped after that performance. However, the pacer has made a strong comeback on the ongoing New Zealand tour.
Kamboj made his ODI debut against the West Indies on October 3, 2026. He then impressed in the first ODI against New Zealand in Auckland on November 4, taking 2 wickets for 22 runs. His performance earned him the Player of the Match award. He continued his good form in the second ODI in Wellington on November 7, picking up 2 wickets for 25 runs.
Shastri believes Kamboj's ability to move the ball in both directions and trouble batters makes him a valuable option.
"More importantly, if there is something there in the surface, the ball will nibble, he hits the bat, and he can get the ball to go both ways and surprise the batter. I think a welcome addition. You have got to build your bench strength as a fast bowling unit, and I think he is one of them. For New Zealand, South Africa, and England, he becomes a good choice," Shastri said.

briefs.headline: Gill-Rahul out, Kishan-Gaikwad in? Rayudu, Karthik predict India's changes
briefs.deck: With Shubman Gill and KL Rahul set to miss the final two games to prepare for the upcoming Test series, the spotlight now shifts to the batting combination Shreyas Iyer will field in the remaining matches. Former India cricketers Ambati Rayudu and Dinesh Karthik have backed Ishan Kishan and Ruturaj Gaikwad to come into the playing XI, offering India a new-look top and middle order for the final…
briefs.bodyText:
India have already taken an unassailable 2-0 lead in the five-match ODI series against New Zealand, with the third match in Hamilton abandoned due to rain. With 
Shubman Gill
 and KL 
Rahul
 set to miss the final two games to prepare for the upcoming Test series, the spotlight now shifts to the batting combination Shreyas Iyer will field in the remaining matches.
Former India cricketers Ambati Rayudu and Dinesh Karthik have backed 
Ishan Kishan
 and Ruturaj Gaikwad to come into the playing XI, offering India a new-look top and middle order for the final leg of the series.
India take 2-0 lead after two wins, third ODI washed out
India began the series with a five-wicket victory (DLS method) in Auckland on November 4. After bowling New Zealand out for 185 in 40.2 overs, the visitors chased down a revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli top-scored with 74 off 51 balls, while Anshul Kamboj was named Player of the Match for his two-wicket haul.
The second ODI in Wellington proved to be a much tighter contest. New Zealand were dismissed for 134 in 41 overs, with Gurnoor Brar leading India's bowling effort with figures of 4/30. India were 113/7 in 26 overs when rain interrupted play, but had moved four runs ahead of the DLS par score to secure a four-run victory. Shreyas Iyer scored 30, while KL Rahul remained unbeaten on 26.
The third ODI at Seddon Park in Hamilton on November 10 was abandoned without a ball being bowled due to persistent rain. 
India had won the toss and elected to bowl, but repeated delays and ground inspections eventually forced the officials to call off the contest.
The result ensured India retained their 2-0 advantage in the series, with the final two matches scheduled to be played in Mount Maunganui on November 13 and 15.
Rayudu backs Ishan Kishan, Ruturaj Gaikwad for playing XI
With Gill unavailable for the remaining matches, Ishan Kishan is a strong candidate to open alongside Rohit Sharma. The left-handed wicketkeeper-batter is also the designated vice-captain for the final two ODIs, making his inclusion a likely option.
Rayudu believes Kishan should replace Gill at the top, while Gaikwad should get an opportunity in the middle order in place of Rahul. He also pointed out that Gaikwad's recent role in the Indian side has not been as an opener.
"I would go with Ishan Kishan to replace Shubman Gill at the top and open with Rohit Sharma. Ruturaj Gaikwad has scored a 100, but he has not opened for India in recent times," Rayudu said on Cricbuzz.
"I think Ishan Kishan and Ruturaj Gaikwad should be coming into the playing XI, and they can be moved up and down according to what number you would like them to bat," he added.
Karthik echoed Rayudu's suggestions, backing Kishan at the top and Gaikwad in the middle order. He also highlighted the left-right batting combination that the two changes could offer India.
"I think Ishan may be at the top, and you have played Rutu in the middle order, so he comes in for KL Rahul. You will get the left-right combination as well," Karthik said.
Karthik raises question over Anshul Kamboj's replacement
Karthik also discussed India's bowling options for the remaining matches, with Anshul Kamboj absent from the revised squad.
He raised the possibility of giving Yash Thakur an opportunity or bringing Mohammed Siraj into the playing XI.
"Does Yash Thakur get a gig? Or does Mohammed Siraj come in? I hope he gets a game. So, Gill, Rahul, and Kamboj have left the playing XI, so you have three ready-made replacements in the playing XI," Karthik added.

briefs.headline: Donna Kelce On Travis' Bond: family says nieces rule his visits; Kylie calls oldest the boss
briefs.deck: Travis Kelce, the popular quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs' bond with his nieces has mae his mother Donna Kelce emotional.
briefs.bodyText:
Travis Kelce
, the popular quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs, might be one of the best athletes in the league but he has also been a complete family man. The star player has always been incredibly close to both his parents and to his brother, Jason Kelce, his wife Kylie Kelce and their four daughters. Amid this, Travis Kelce’s mother Donna Kelce opens up on an emotional moment concerning Travis Kelce.
Travis Kelce’s mother Donna Kelce reflects on how the tight end has formed a special bond with Jason Kelce’s daughters
In an interview with PEOPLE, Travis Kelce and Jason Kelce’s mother, Donna Kelce, reflected on the bond that the popular tight end shares with his four nieces as she said, "It's kind of like a free-for-all where he's throwing them up in the air and on the couch…”
Travis Kelce’s mother added, “Jason does the same thing. It's just amazing to see your grown-up children interact with their own kids. It's very heartwarming."
Interestingly, even Jason Kelce’s wife Kylie Kelce has been public about how Travis Kelce has been able to build a pretty close bond with all four of his nieces.
In an interview with PEOPLE, the Not Gonna Lie host Kylie Kelce reflected on their special bond as she said, "I tell everybody, he comes to our house to visit and the poor guy doesn't sit on the couch because our daughters will be like, 'No, no, you sit on the floor. We're gonna do a puzzle. We're gonna build blocks. We're gonna do this, we're gonna do that.' "
Jason Kelce’s wife Kylie Kelce added, "Our oldest, she's our boss. She's our ring leader, and she just has demand after demand for him. And I'm like, 'Trav, you know you can tell Wyatt no?' "
While the Kansas City Chiefs’ star player Travis Kelce has no children of his own, he has always been able to form a quick bond with his nieces.
In many of the matches in the last few years, all four of his nieces have shown up to cheer on Travis Kelce.
Travis Kelce remains committed to his career amid Kansas City Chiefs’ minor setback on the field
While Travis Kelce has been focused on his career for the last decade, he has always prioritised his family over his achievements on the field.
For now, all eyes remain on the 37 year old tight end as he breaks records on the field after the Kansas City Chiefs bounced back on the field amid two back to back losses.
After a disappointing run on the field in the last season, this season has been incredibly rewarding for Travis Kelce as he has broken records in the first few matches.

briefs.headline: F1 season to end in Qatar, Abu Dhabi as scheduled
briefs.deck: The teams competing in the championship have been informed of the decision, with Formula One saying all 11 ‌were supportive
briefs.bodyText:
Formula One will end its season in West Asia as scheduled with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, the Liberty Media-owned sport said on Tuesday with Italy’s Imola circuit no longer required as a backup option.
The teams competing in the championship have been informed of the decision, with Formula One saying all 11 were supportive.
The move comes after MotoGP held its Qatar round at the Lusail circuit near Doha last weekend.
Both Formula One championships have been decided, with 20-year-old Italian Kimi Antonelli taking the drivers’ title as youngest ever champion in Mexico this month and his Mercedes team completing the double in Brazil last Sunday.
Imola was a fallback option, pencilled in for December 6 should the Iran war and regional conflict make it unsafe for Formula One to complete its calendar of Qatar on November 29 and Abu Dhabi the weekend after.
Home venue
The Italian circuit — a home venue for Antonelli and also for Ferrari — had a cutoff point, however, and local organisers were informed of the decision on Tuesday.
“We are ready for Qatar and Abu Dhabi,” International Automobile Federation (FIA) president Mohammed Ben Sulayem posted on Instagram.
“We are fully prepared and committed to delivering two outstanding grand prix weekends and a spectacular conclusion to the FIA Formula One world championship,” added the Emirati.
“We look forward to welcoming drivers, teams and fans to two iconic circuits for an unforgettable finish to the season.”
The decision means the F1 calendar will be 23 rounds and that the Formula Two feeder series will be decided on the track, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi hosting the remaining races.
Brazilian Rafael Camara, who made his Formula One race debut with Haas in his home race at the weekend, leads Red Bull-backed Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov by seven points.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday he planned to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar’s prime minister.
Formula One could still cancel the races if the situation flares up, with safety a priority. The next race is in Las Vegas on November 21.

briefs.headline: Bayern coach Vincent Kompany returns to club for first time since collapse
briefs.deck: The 40-year-old Kompany had medical treatment scheduled at the Säbener Strasse complex as he took another step toward his planned return after the international break
briefs.bodyText:
Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany has returned to the club’s training ground for the first time since he collapsed during practice last month. Bayern also revealed he suffered a shoulder injury.
The 40-year-old Kompany had medical treatment scheduled at the Säbener Strasse complex as he took another step toward his planned return after the international break.
“Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground at Säbener Strasse since the start of the week,” the club said on Tuesday. “The FC Bayern head coach is also completing rehab on his injured shoulder there. Kompany was under medical care recently, with assistant coach Aaron Danks filling in.”
Bayern had no team training on Tuesday with most of the players away. The team’s next game is at home to Cologne in the Bundesliga on Nov. 20.
Bayern powerbroker Uli Hoeness said on Sunday that Kompany would return in time for that match.
Kompany collapsed while observing a training session on Oct. 23 and was hospitalized for meningeal irritation, an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord. He had been dealing with a viral infection and hip injury.
Danks took charge of the team while Kompany was away and oversaw wins against Freiburg, Magdeburg, Atlético Madrid and Mainz with the only blot a 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund in der Klassiker on October 31.

briefs.headline: Savita makes way for Bansari in Indian women’s hockey squad for ACT
briefs.deck: India will begin their campaign against Malaysia on the opening day of the competition
briefs.bodyText:
Veteran goalkeeper Savita Punia has been rested from the Asian Champions Trophy in Bhopal, replaced by Bansari Solanki in the Indian women's hockey squad unveiled on Tuesday, with head coach Sjoerd Marijne also announcing changes to the roles of some players during the event.
The tournament is scheduled to be held from November 19 to 28 at the newly-built International Sports Complex, Nathu Barkheda, Bhopal and India will enter as the defending champions. India will begin their campaign against Malaysia on the opening day of the competition.
Mid-fielder Salima Tete will continue to lead the team, which is playing its first international tournament after the historic gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan last month.
The hosts have secured the ACT title in 2016, 2023 and 2024.
The six-team competition will feature India, China, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and South Korea. Like India, South Korea too have won the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy three times.
The 25-year-old Bansari has been part of the squad that won the Asia Cup last year. Bichu Devi Kharibam retained her place as the other custodian in the squad.
"This is the moment I want to give other players the chance to showcase their talent on the international stage. Some players will be playing in different positions than they normally do, so that I can see how they perform in a different role," said Marijne.
"We are excited to play in front of the home crowd and finish the year well," he added.
As part of the role shuffling, Rutuja Dadaso Pisal, who played as a forward in the Asian Games, has been named in the mid-field for the ACT. Similarly, mid-fielder Nikki Pradhan is part of the defensive line-up, while Ishika Chaudhary has been moved from defence to mid-field.
The ACT will follow a round-robin format, with each team playing the other five once. The top four teams at the end of the league stage will qualify for the semi-finals.
The opening day will see Asia's top-ranked team China take on Thailand in the tournament opener before the India-Malaysia clash following an opening ceremony.
The Indian team will then face South Korea on November 21, Thailand on November 22, China on November 24 and Japan on November 25.
The semi-finals will be played on November 27 and the medal matches on November 28.
With the home crowd behind them, the Indian team will look to deliver another strong performance and continue their winning momentum.
"The Women's Asian Champions Trophy Bhopal 2026 is an important opportunity for our team to carry forward the momentum of their historic Asian Games triumph," said Hockey India President Dilip Tirkey.
"Playing in front of home supporters will be a great motivation, and I am confident the players will put up a strong performance and make the country proud," he added.
Hockey India Secretary General, Bhola Nath Singh, also wished the team success in the tournament.
"As defending champions, the team will be determined to maintain its winning momentum. We look forward to an exciting competition and strong support from hockey fans across Madhya Pradesh," said the Secretary General.

Defenders: Nikki Pradhan, Jyoti, Jyoti Singh, Sushila Chanu, Lalthantluangi, Pooja Sahoo
Mid-fielders: Rutuja Dadaso Pisal, Sunelita Toppo, Salima Tete (c), Neha, Sakshi Rana, Baljeeet Kaur, Ishika.
Forwards: Navneet Kaur, Deepika, Beauty Dungdung, Lalremsiami, Mumtaz Khan.

briefs.headline: India A-New Zealand A series ends in draw after rain washes out fourth day of third unofficial Test
briefs.deck: All three four-day matches failed to produce a result
briefs.bodyText:
The third and final unofficial Test between India A and New Zealand A ended in a draw, with the series ending in a draw.
All three four-day matches failed to produce a result. At the end of day 4, NZ A was 36/2, with Dean Foxcroft (10*) and Zak Gibson (1*) unbeaten. They trailed by 428 runs.
Earlier, New Zealand A won the toss and elected to field first.
A 175-run opening stand between Yashasvi Jaiswal (102 in 138 balls, with 16 fours and two sixes) and Sai Sudharsan (88 in 215 balls, with 11 fours) started off things for India.
Half-centuries came from the bat of Tilak Varma (81 in 164 balls, with five fours and two sixes), skipper Dhruv Jurel (71 in 95 balls, with nine fours and two sixes) and Washington Sundar (50* in 107 balls, with two fours) as India posted 464/5.
Zak Gibson (2/73) was the leading wicket-taker for NZ.
India’s batting was a big plus ahead of the Test series starting on November 19, with Devdutt Padikkal (326 runs in three matches and five innings at an average of 65.20, with a century and a fifty) being the top run-scorer. After a few poor scores, Yashasvi Jaiswal (279 runs in three matches and five innings at an average of 69.75, with two centuries) also scored back-to-back tons.
Sai Sudharsan (231 runs in three matches and five innings at an average of 46.20, with two fifties) and skipper Jurel (179 runs in three matches and four innings at an average of 44.75, with a century and a fifty) also played some fine knocks for India. Uncapped batter Yash Rathod (223 runs in two matches at an average of 111.50, with a century and a fifty) also was a big positive for India.
Auqib Nabi (six wickets in a match) and Mohammed Siraj (four wickets in a match) were the leading wicket-takers for India.
India Test squad for two NZ Tests: Shubman Gill [C], Yashasvi Jaiswal, KL Rahul [VC], Devdutt Padikkal, Rishabh Pant [WK]*, Dhruv Jurel [WK], Ravindra Jadeja, Anshul Kamboj, Jasprit Bumrah, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep, Sai Sudharsan, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Washington Sundar, Kuldeep Yadav, Mohammed Siraj.
